prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, bringing optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level.

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is a clear, original idea (trap many neutral atoms at a magic wavelength so that the light shift cancels on the clock transition) that was turned into an instrument whose accuracy and stability have improved by orders of magnitude over microwave standards. It has been reproduced and surpassed by independent laboratories in several countries and species, clock-to-clock comparisons agree at the 10^-18 level, and it is driving the redefinition of the second, relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and dark-sector searches. Attribution is unusually clean: Katori proposed the concept and built the first strontium lattice clock, and Ye's group carried it to the record systematic uncertainty and stability and to many-body clock physics. After the openings I still rank it first. The fact that three of us placed it first is not my reason; my reason is that the discovery is complete, verified and has a precise origin.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with earlier recognition. The 2005 prize (Hall and Haensch, frequency combs) and the 2012 prize (Wineland and Haroche, control of single quantum systems, including ion clocks) cover adjacent technology, so the committee could judge that the optical-clock programme is a refinement of already honoured ideas. There is also a timing argument for waiting until the redefinition of the second is settled, and a genuine question whether the Paris, Boulder and Tokyo groups, and the Yb and Al+ clock communities, are fairly represented by two names.

responses.point: Johansson ranks optical lattice clocks only sixth, regards the two-name attribution as clean but notes that the comb prize of 2005 recognised an adjacent technique, and puts circuit QED first because of its influence on quantum processors.
responses.response: I accept the 2005 point as a real qualification, but the comb is the ruler and the lattice clock is a new kind of oscillator: the magic-wavelength condition, Lamb-Dicke confinement of thousands of atoms and the resulting stability are not consequences of the comb. I disagree that circuit QED should lead. The 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects in circuits is close in subject, and the attribution of circuit QED is harder (four credited names, three seats, Girvin and Blais in tension), whereas the clock has a clean two-person split. I would keep circuit QED as a strong alternative, not the first choice.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp topological insulator work first as a deep and arguably overdue concept with more than fifteen years of independent confirmation.
responses.response: I agree that the topological insulator is conceptually the deeper of the two ideas, and I do not equate the support of my AMO colleagues with merit. But the credit chain is the problem: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe realisation that Molenkamp's group then observed, and they are not among the credited names, so a Kane-Mele-Molenkamp prize would leave out a decisive link, and the 2016 prize already touches topological phases. I would take it forward as my first alternative, and I would change my ranking if the committee found a defensible way to settle the attribution.

responses.point: Eriksson places twisted bilayer graphene first, arguing that the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction and the 2018 discovery created a broad field with a clean theory-plus-experiment pairing.
responses.response: The prediction-plus-discovery pairing is attractive and I take the field's breadth seriously. My hesitation is maturity: the origin of the superconductivity is still debated and the experimental credit is narrower than the work (Cao, Fatemi and others in the same group are not named), so I think this is not yet as settled as the clock. I would not rank it ahead of a result whose performance can be checked against independent clocks.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the lattice clock first because it is the clearest case where a laser-spectroscopy technique has changed what can be measured, with many independent labs surpassing each other, while noting that Hall, Haensch and Wineland already recognised adjacent work.
responses.response: I agree with the maturity and reproducibility argument, and I share the concern about adjacent prizes. Where I qualify his view is on Ye's role: I would describe it as the leading realisation and the systematic-uncertainty record, which is a distinct achievement from Katori's proposal. I therefore favour a citation that credits both the concept and the realisation, which is what a two-name prize does.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges optical lattice clocks sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 trapped-ion prizes.
Whether the prize should wait for the redefinition of the second.
Whether two names fairly represent contributions from other groups (Paris, Boulder, Tokyo, ytterbium and aluminium-ion clocks).
Whether a topological insulator prize can be configured with Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang outside the credited list.
statement.conflict_note: No direct connection to Katori or Ye is documented in my profile. As a theorist of atomic structure I work in the same broad area, and my profile documents collaborations with Anne L'Huillier, the Lund attosecond group and Ursula Keller's ETH group, none of whom are credited on the ballots I propose. I do not see a specific conflict for B046 or the alternatives, but I flag the closeness of atomic physics to this topic for the committee to judge.
